newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Drought could hit Tanzanian economic gains, IMF. [CORRECTED 16:40 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Drought could hit Tanzanian economic gains, IMF. [CORRECTED 16:40 GMT]

text.p: Prolonged drought in Tanzania could hurt its hard-won economic gains, an International Monetary Fund official said on Friday.
Goodall Gondwe, deputy director of the Africa department, told Reuters in an interview if the drought was prolonged it would harm Tanzania's ability to repay its foreign debt.
"All these results...where Tanzania has done well could in fact quite quickly change as a result of the drought. We're hoping very much rain will come and we won't have a drought," he said.

But Gondwe said a dramatic reduction in earnings from coffee exports, Tanzania's biggest source of foreign exchange, should not change its debt repayment schedule. Tanzania's foreign debt stands at $7.6 billion.

Earnings from coffee are expected to drop in the current 1996/97 season to some 42,000 tonnes worth $95 million from a production peak averaging 55,160 tonnes (corrects from 5,160 tonnes) between 1981 and 1985.
Drought is a major reason for the decline, particularly among the premium mild washed arabicas grown in northern Moshi.
Gondwe said a decision late last year by the Paris Club of creditor nations led to reductions in Tanzania's annual debt repayment from $404 million in 1995/96 to $140 million in 1996/97.
Interest rate payments had also fallen from $152 million in 1995/96 to $107 million in 1996/97, he added.
He said an IMF team would visit Kenya in April to assess progress on implementing agreed benchmarks for an Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF) package of loans.
"There are certain benchmarks unlike Tanzania which have not been done. An IMF mission will go back to Kenya next month to complete its review," Gondwe said.
He said statements that Tanzania was the weakest of the three main East African economies were not necessarily true.
He said Tanzania's foreign currency reserves were almost equal to Kenya's and much bigger than Uganda's.

"As far as Tanzania's reserves are concerned they're comparable to Kenyas and higher then Uganda, so its economy is not weak -- only it's a large country and they (the government) could do more. They're not tapping its potential," Gondwe said.
